# Instructor information

| | |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Peter Fuleky |

| **Office hours** | By appointment — in person or via Zoom |

# Course description

This course gives economists a working command of the two dominant
empirical traditions in modern economics: **prediction** (statistical /
machine learning and time-series forecasting) and **causal inference**
(research design for estimating treatment effects from observational data).

The first two-thirds of the course build a supervised- and unsupervised-learning
toolkit and a time-series forecasting toolkit, following *An Introduction to
Statistical Learning* (ISLR) and two time-series chapters from Verbeek. The
final third pivots from "what will happen?" to "what *causes* what?", following
Nick Huntington-Klein's *The Effect*.

# Learning outcomes

By the end of the course students will be able to:

1. Fit, tune, and honestly evaluate supervised-learning models (regression and
   classification) using resampling, regularization, and flexible methods.
2. Apply tree-based methods, support vector machines, deep learning, and
   unsupervised methods, and choose appropriately among them.
3. Model and forecast economic time series (ARMA, unit roots) and
   multivariate systems (VAR, cointegration, VECM).
4. Translate an economic question into a research design, express identifying
   assumptions with causal diagrams (DAGs), and reason about back-door paths.
5. Estimate causal effects with regression, matching, fixed effects, event
   studies, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and regression
   discontinuity — and state when each is credible.
6. Carry out all of the above in **R** with the `tidymodels` / `tidyverse`
   ecosystem and the standard econometrics packages.
7. Prepare and deliver a short lecture on a technical topic and guide the
   class discussion that follows — building teaching and presentation
   skills through the course's flipped-classroom format.

# Format and pacing

In-person, meeting **Tuesdays and Thursdays, 9:00–10:15 am**, in the
classroom. Instruction runs **08/25 through 12/10**, with the final exam during
the **12/14–12/18** examination period. This is a **flipped
classroom**: you prepare before each session — reading, watching the video
lecture, and reviewing the lecture notes for that day's topic — and one
enrolled student leads the session by delivering a short lecture on the
topic, analyzing labs/exercises and initiating class discussion. The
instructor's role is to guide that discussion, not to carry a lecture. There are more class sessions over the
semester than students enrolled, so everyone will sign up to lead multiple
sessions; sign-ups will be arranged early in the term. Each week's assigned
topic spans both weekly sessions — one to present the material and open
discussion, the other to continue discussion, work through labs/exercises,
and answer questions.

Beyond covering the technical material, repeatedly preparing and leading a
session is meant to build your teaching and presentation skills — explaining
technical content clearly, anticipating questions, and facilitating a
discussion — skills that transfer directly to seminars, job talks, and
teaching of your own.

# Prerequisites

An introductory econometrics course (OLS, hypothesis testing) and basic
statistics. No prior R is assumed — the ISLR labs in Weeks 1–3 ramp up R
skills gently alongside a gentle statistics review, so the course is
self-onboarding. Comfort with algebra and basic calculus notation is expected.

# Materials

## Primary text — the source textbooks

Read the assigned chapter in the original text first. ISLR and *The Effect* are
free online; for the two time-series chapters, where the source (Verbeek) is not
freely available, the lecture notes serve as the primary reading instead.

- James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani, *An Introduction to Statistical Learning*
  (2nd ed.), Ch 1–13 — free PDF and resources at [statlearning.com](https://www.statlearning.com/).
- Huntington-Klein, *The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and
  Causality* — full text free online at [theeffectbook.net](https://theeffectbook.net/).
- Verbeek, *A Guide to Modern Econometrics* (5th ed.), Ch 8–9 — the source for
  the time-series chapters. Not freely available; the lecture notes cover this
  material in full, and the companion data for labs will be provided. Additional
  online resources include [Forecasting: Principles and Practice](https://otexts.com/fpp3/),
  and [STAT 510: Applied Time Series Analysis](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat510/).

## Review — the instructor's lecture notes

After the original chapter and the videos, use these lecture notes to
consolidate your understanding. They are self-contained, include all lab
code, worked exercises, and a *Further Reading* section of landmark applied
papers per chapter. Each set of notes is a searchable website, with the full
text also downloadable as a PDF or EPUB from the site's *Downloads* section.

- **[Prediction & time series notes](https://special-adventure-gw99jmk.pages.github.io/)**
  — *Lecture Notes for ISLR and Time Series*, covering ISLR Ch 1–13 and Verbeek
  time series Ch 14–15.
- **[Causal inference notes](https://fantastic-adventure-v611vgo.pages.github.io/)**
  — *Lecture Notes for The Effect*, covering research design and causal methods.

::: {.callout-important}
## You need a GitHub account to read the notes

Both notes sites are private to this class. Sign in to [GitHub](https://github.com/)
with the account you give me at the start of the semester, and I will grant you
access; the sites then open normally. If you are not signed in, or your account
has not been added yet, you will be redirected to a GitHub login page instead of
the notes. Create a free account before the first session and send me your
username — no institutional email is required. You will need the same account to
post in Discussions and to submit homework (see *Communications* and *Assessment*).
:::

## Companion video lectures (free)

| Module | Video source | Link |
|--------|--------------|------|
| ISLR (Ch 1–13) | Stanford *Statistical Learning* — Hastie, Tibshirani & Witten | [statlearning.com](https://www.statlearning.com/) · [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLOg0ngHtcqbPTlZzRHA2ocQZqB1D_qZ5V) |
| Time series (Verbeek Ch 14–15) | Ben Lambert — *Time Series* (ARMA, unit roots, VAR, cointegration); *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* (ARIMA, decomposition, exponential smoothing) | [Lambert](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLvo9ZnEQG5oXC-cg8ecXr6SJZWprEL1UC) · [FPP](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLyCNZ_xXGzpm7W9jLqbIyBAiSO5jDwJeE) |
| Causal inference (*The Effect*) | Nick Huntington-Klein — *The Effect: Videos on Causal Inference* (episode-mapped to chapters) | [nickchk.com/videos](https://nickchk.com/videos.html) |

The two author video series (ISLR, *The Effect*) track our chapters almost
one-to-one. The time-series chapters are the only place we rely on third-party
video (Lambert and *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*).

## Software (free)

[R](https://cran.r-project.org/) + [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/), with
`tidymodels`, `tidyverse`, `ISLR2`, and the engine packages used in the labs
(`glmnet`, `xgboost`, `randomForest`, `kernlab`, `rpart`, `keras3`), plus the
time-series packages (`forecast`, `tseries`, `vars`, `urca`) and the
causal packages (`fixest`, `did`, `rdrobust`, `AER`, `MatchIt`). The notes ship
an `renv` lockfile; `renv::restore()` installs everything at pinned versions.

# How each week works

Every week follows the same rhythm, whether or not you are leading that
week's session:

1. **Read** the assigned chapter in the original textbook - ~2-3 hrs.
2. **Watch** the assigned video lecture(s) - ~2 hrs.
3. **Review** your understanding by reading the corresponding lecture notes - ~1-2 hrs.
4. **Run** the lab code yourself (the `.R` scripts mirror every code
   chunk; edit and re-run them) - ~2 hrs.
5. **Self-check** the coding and applied exercises against the provided
   solutions - ~2 hrs.
6. **Write up, by hand,** a short summary of the week's material and your
   solutions to the conceptual exercises, and submit it by Sunday 8 pm
   ~2 hrs.
7. **Present or discuss in class.** If you are leading a session this week,
   turn steps 1–6 into a short lecture. Either way, come to both the
   Tuesday and Thursday sessions ready to discuss the material.

The hand-written submission (step 6) is collected; the labs and coding
exercises in steps 4–5 are self-check practice, but are also analyzed and
discussed in the classroom sessions.

# Schedule

Three blocks, each ending in an exam. Each week's topic is covered across
both of that week's sessions — the Tuesday session is a student-led lecture
on the assigned chapter plus opening discussion, and the Thursday session
continues discussion, works through labs/exercises, and answers questions.
The sign-up for who presents which week is arranged separately (see *Format
and pacing*); the tables below show the fixed topics and readings,
independent of who presents them.

- **Block I** → Midterm 1
- **Block II** → Midterm 2
- **Block III** → Final (causal material only)

**No class on Tue 11/03 (Election Day) or Thu 11/26 (Thanksgiving)** — both are
University non-instructional days. That leaves 30 meetings between the first
session on 08/25 and the last on 12/10, so two weeks run as a single session:
Week 6, shortened to make room for Midterm 1, and Week 13, shortened by
Thanksgiving. Week 11 keeps both of its sessions, but they straddle a weekend
(Thu 11/05 and Tue 11/10) because Election Day removes its Tuesday.

## Block I — Supervised learning → Midterm 1

| Week | Dates | Notes | Topic | Video |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tue 08/25 · Thu 08/27 | ISLR 1 + 2 | Course intro; statistical learning, bias–variance, KNN; R onboarding starts | StatLearning Ch 1–2 |
| 2 | Tue 09/01 · Thu 09/03 | ISLR 3 | Linear regression (revisited in Block III) | StatLearning Ch 3 |
| 3 | Tue 09/08 · Thu 09/10 | ISLR 4 | Classification: logistic, LDA/QDA, naive Bayes | StatLearning Ch 4 |
| 4 | Tue 09/15 · Thu 09/17 | ISLR 5 | Resampling: cross-validation & the bootstrap (simulation revisited in Block III) | StatLearning Ch 5 |
| 5 | Tue 09/22 · Thu 09/24 | ISLR 6 | Model selection & regularization: subset selection, ridge, lasso | StatLearning Ch 6 |
| 6 | Tue 09/29 *(one session)* | ISLR 7 | Moving beyond linearity: polynomials, splines, GAMs | StatLearning Ch 7 |

: **Midterm 1 — Thu 10/01**, in class. Covers ISLR Ch 1–7.

## Block II — Advanced ML & time series → Midterm 2

| Week | Dates | Notes | Topic | Video |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Tue 10/06 · Thu 10/08 | ISLR 8 | Tree-based methods: trees, random forests, boosting, BART | StatLearning Ch 8 |
| 8 | Tue 10/13 · Thu 10/15 | ISLR 9 + 12 | Support vector machines; unsupervised learning (PCA, *k*-means, hierarchical) | StatLearning Ch 9, 12 |
| 9 | Tue 10/20 · Thu 10/22 | ISLR 10 | Deep learning: feed-forward nets, CNNs, RNNs | StatLearning Ch 10 |
| 10 | Tue 10/27 · Thu 10/29 | Verbeek 14 | Univariate time series: ARMA, unit roots, forecasting | Lambert, FPP (ARIMA & forecasting) |
| 11 | Thu 11/05 · Tue 11/10 *(no class Tue 11/03, Election Day)* | Verbeek 15 | Multivariate time series: VAR, Granger causality, IRFs, cointegration, VECM | Lambert (VAR & cointegration) |

: **Midterm 2 — Thu 11/12**, in class. Covers ISLR Ch 8–12 + Time Series Ch 14–15.

Note the compressed run-up: Week 11's second session is **Tue 11/10**, two days
before the exam. Multivariate time series is the densest material in the block, so
do not leave it until the last week — the weekly rhythm exists precisely so that
exam preparation is review rather than first contact.

*Optional self-study (not on any exam):* ISLR 11 (Survival Analysis) and ISLR 13
(Multiple Testing) remain in the notes for interested students.

## Block III — Causal inference → Final

| Week | Dates | Notes | Topic | Video (*The Effect*) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | Tue 11/17 · Thu 11/19 | Effect 5–8 + 10 | Identification; causal diagrams (DAGs); drawing diagrams; closing back doors; treatment effects (ATE/ATT/LATE) | Identification → Treatment Effects |
| 13 | Tue 11/24 *(one session — no class Thu 11/26, Thanksgiving)* | Effect 13 + 14 | Regression *as causal adjustment* (re-frames ISLR 3); matching | Regression, Matching |
| 14 | Tue 12/01 · Thu 12/03 | Effect 16 + 17 + 18 | Fixed effects; event studies; difference-in-differences | Fixed Effects, Event Studies, DiD |
| 15 | Tue 12/08 · Thu 12/10 | Effect 19 + 20 | Instrumental variables; regression discontinuity | IV, RDD |

: **Final Exam** — during the **12/14–12/18** examination period; the exact slot
comes from the Registrar's final examination schedule and will be posted in
*Announcements*. Covers the causal material from *The Effect* only.

**How the prediction and causal parts connect.** Week 12 front-loads the
conceptual design material — identification, causal diagrams, back-door paths,
and the definitions of treatment effects — so that Weeks 13–15 are pure method.
Effect Ch 13 (regression) is taught as a *causal re-interpretation* of the OLS
machinery from ISLR Ch 3, not from scratch.

# Assessment

| Component | When | Coverage | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weekly homework | Sundays, 8 pm | Hand-written, all 15 weeks | 10% |
| Presentation & participation | Throughout | Leading assigned sessions; discussion engagement | 30% |
| Midterm 1 | **Thu 10/01**, in class | ISLR Ch 1–7 | 20% |
| Midterm 2 | **Thu 11/12**, in class | ISLR Ch 8–12 + Time Series Ch 14–15 | 20% |
| Final Exam | **12/14–12/18**, slot TBA | Causal inference (*The Effect*) only | 20% |

**Homework (10%).** A hand-written summary of the week's study material and your
solutions to the conceptual exercises, submitted every week by Sunday 8 pm.
Write the work out by hand, then scan it (or photograph it) and submit it as a
single PDF. Writing by hand aids retention and confirms steady weekly
engagement. The coding and applied exercises are self-checked against the
provided solutions and are not collected.

Submission goes through **GitHub Classroom**: each week you accept an invitation
link (posted in *Announcements*) and receive a repository that only you and the
instructor can see. Upload the PDF through the GitHub website — **Add file →
Upload files** — and commit. You never need to install Git or use a terminal.
Each assignment has a cutoff at the deadline, after which the repository becomes
read-only, so the no-late-work policy is enforced automatically rather than at my
discretion. Full instructions live in `assignments/README.md` in the course
repository.

**Presentation & participation (30%).** Each student signs up to lead
multiple class sessions over the semester — there are more class sessions
than students enrolled, so everyone leads more than one. When leading a
session, prepare and deliver a short lecture on that day's topic (using the
reading, videos, and lecture notes as source material), then guide the
discussion that follows; the instructor's role is to facilitate, not to
lecture. Grading considers preparation, clarity of the lecture, and the
quality of the discussion you draw out of your classmates. The remainder of
the grade reflects active participation in every other session — asking
questions and engaging with the presenter's material.

**Exams (20% each).** Each exam is **closed-book, closed-notes, and
timed**, held in the classroom and proctored by the instructor. Exams combine
conceptual short-answer items with applied "interpret-this-output" questions.

The two midterms are given during a regular class session — **Thu 10/01** and
**Thu 11/12** — so they take the usual 75 minutes. The **Final** is scheduled in
the University's examination period, **12/14–12/18**; the exact day and time come
from the Registrar's final examination schedule and will be posted in
*Announcements* once published. Do not book travel for that week until it is.

# Course policies

## Late work

No late homework is accepted. The weekly hand-written submission is due
**Sunday 8 pm**; this firm deadline is what makes the weekly homework a
reliable signal of steady engagement (see *How each week works*). The submission
repository becomes read-only at the deadline, so submit an incomplete write-up
rather than nothing.

## Withdrawal

Add/drop and withdrawal deadlines follow the University's academic calendar —
see the [UH Mānoa Academic Calendar](https://manoa.hawaii.edu/registrar/academic-calendar/)
for the current semester's specific dates for dropping without a "W" and for
withdrawing from the course.

## Extra credit

None.

## Communications

Course announcements and Q&A go through **GitHub Discussions** in the course
repository, `uh-manoa-uhero/econ630`, using three categories:

- **Announcements** — schedule changes, exam logistics, corrections to the
  lecture notes, and assignment links. Instructor-posted; watch the repository so
  these reach you by email.
- **Q&A** — questions about chapters, labs, and exercises. Post here rather than
  emailing, so the whole class benefits from the answer. Answering a classmate
  counts toward your participation grade.
- **Presentation sign-ups** — one pinned thread where you claim the sessions you
  will lead. The resulting schedule is kept in `presentations.md` in the
  repository.

Everything in Discussions is visible to the whole class, so do not post graded
work there — homework is submitted privately (see *Assessment*).

For anything personal — grades, accommodations, access problems — email
`fuleky@hawaii.edu`; expect a response within 24 hours. Office hours are held by
appointment, in person or via Zoom.

# AI and outside resources policy

Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) may be used throughout the course —
including on the weekly homework, the lab/coding exercises, and preparing
your presentation — as a **learning tool**: to help you understand material,
debug code, or check your reasoning. Keep in mind that AI is not failproof and 
generated content requires verification. **AI use is not permitted during
exams.** All exams are closed-book, closed-notes, and taken under
supervision (see *Assessment*). Submitted homework and in-class lectures must
still reflect your own understanding: if you cannot explain or reproduce a
solution — or field your classmates' questions about it — you have not
actually learned the material the exams will test you on.

# Course technology

Course materials (lecture notes, labs, assignments, schedule) are distributed
through the course repository `uh-manoa-uhero/econ630` and the two lecture-note
websites linked under *Materials*. The following tools are used:

- **GitHub** hosts the course repository, the lecture notes, announcements and
  Q&A (Discussions), and homework submission (Classroom). A free account is
  required; no institutional email is needed
  ([Accessibility](https://accessibility.github.com/),
  [Privacy Statement](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement)).
- **Zoom** is used for office hours held remotely
  ([Accessibility Statement](https://zoom.us/accessibility), [Privacy Policy](https://zoom.us/privacy)).

The hand-written weekly homework is scanned or photographed and uploaded as a
single PDF to your private GitHub Classroom repository for that week; see
*Assessment* for the procedure.

## Required hardware and software

- A laptop able to run [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) and
  [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/) (see *Materials* for the full
  package list), brought to class for lab walkthroughs and discussion.
- A scanner or smartphone camera and a PDF viewer, for submitting
  hand-written homework.

## Minimum technical skill requirements

Comfort with basic computer skills — installing software, using a web
browser, and downloading/uploading/scanning files — is assumed. No prior
programming experience is required; see *Prerequisites*. **No knowledge of Git or
version control is required either** — GitHub is used here only as a website: you
click links, read pages, post in Discussions, and upload a PDF through a web form.

## Academic honesty

Acts of dishonesty, including but not limited to the following:

- Cheating, plagiarism, or other forms of academic dishonesty.

Cheating is an act of academic dishonesty and includes, but is not limited to:

1. use of any unauthorized assistance in taking quizzes, tests, or
   examinations;
2. use of sources beyond those authorized by the instructor in writing
   papers, preparing reports, solving problems, or carrying out other
   assignments;
3. the acquisition, without permission, of tests or other academic material
   belonging to a member of the UH faculty, staff or student body; and
4. engaging in any behavior specifically prohibited by a faculty member in
   the course syllabus or class discussion.

Plagiarism is also an act of academic dishonesty and includes, but is not
limited to:

- the use, by paraphrase or direct quotation, of the published or
  unpublished work of another person without full and clear acknowledgement.
- It also includes the unacknowledged use of materials prepared by another
  person or agency engaged in the selling of term papers or other academic
  materials.

Furnishing false information to any UH official, faculty member, or office.

Forgery, alteration, or misuse of any UH document, record, or form of
identification.
